column30: The City is mandated under Local Law 22 to compile an annual GHG emissions inventory. There are 4 inventories updated yearly:1.City Government - Municipal Operations Emissions including but not limited to buildings, fleet, water and waste treatment.2.Citywide (GPC) - all activities within the city's limits, including buildings, waste and water treatment, transportation, and power generation.3.Citywide (CLCPA) - all activities within the city's limits including buildings, waste and water treatment, transportation, and power generation, using the methods outlined in the NYC CLCPA to consider upstream impacts from the production of energy to the point of extraction and distribution). In this inventory there is a GWP multiplier that looks at a 20-year timeframe as opposed to the 100-year timeframe industry standard.4.Integrated Citywide & Consumption - measures the emissions from household consumption and integrates that into the Citywide (GPA) inventory for a close to complete view of how New Yorkers drive carbon emissions. (this is a new inventory as of 2021)\n\nWeblink for all historical NYC GHG emissions inventories --> https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/initiatives/nyc-greenhouse-gas-inventories

Attached to this record are Portland's inventory for 2023 in GPC format, Portland's spreadsheet tracking emissions from 1990-2023, and our air travel emissions workbook for 2023.

Portland revised the transportation sector methodology to obtain transportation subsector data. However, there are some data errors showing up this year that we have been unable to resolve. As such the data attached and reported below utilizes our prior transportation methodology (with sources like offroad, rail, and water transport included elsewhere, under the fuel type). The only exception is air travel, which has been attached separately as those emissions were not included elsewhere. Air travel emissions have also been added to the table below. 

For Portland's new transportation methodology, data sets are not available to apply this method to all historic inventories. BPS is currently working on a methodology to reverse forecast those emissions back to the 1990 base year and will submit these inventories to CDP and C40 upon completion. 

In addition, Portland updated all historical inventories with 6th Assessment 100 Yr GWP. We are unable to attach all the historic inventories to this question as they exceed the max file size allowed, but we have attached 2018 through 2022 updated inventories. Please contact us to receive copies of inventories back to 1990.

column30: BISKO emission bugeting includes CO2 and equivalents of N20 and CH4, but it does not include F-gases, yet.In general, F-gases account for 1.3% of Germany's GHG balance. HFCs and PFCs: Used as refrigerants and in industry (e.g. magnesium production). The effort required to record all refrigerant leaks in Heidelberg would be disproportionately high. This might still be conceivable for municipal buildings (air conditioning systems and heat pumps). There, all maintenance logs would have to be recorded centrally and the refill quantities of refrigerants would have to be summed up. The industrial sector plays a minor role in Heidelberg's GHG balance sheet, accounting for 5%. In order to collect HFCs and PFCs, all industrial companies in Heidelberg would have to be surveyed. However, the impact on the GHG balance would probably not be visible. SF6: Occurs in power transmission (e.g. in switchgear) and in industry. So far, SF6 has not been included in the emission factor of the federal electricity mix. If this is the case in the future, SF6 can be included in the upstream emissions of electricity. The same applies to SF6 in industry as to HFCs and PFCs. NF3: Mainly used in the semiconductor industry, for example in the production of flat panel displays and solar cells. Since there is no such production in Heidelberg, it can be assumed that NF3 has no relevance in Heidelberg.

column30:
The community-wide Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions inventory of Ankara Metropolitan Municipality has been prepared to provide a comprehensive overview of emissions across all major sectors and to serve as a foundation for climate mitigation and adaptation planning. The inventory is consistent with the Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventories (GPC) and reported under the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM) Common Reporting Framework (CRF), ensuring international comparability and methodological robustness. This inventory forms an integral part of the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP, 2021), which outlines emission reduction strategies, and is further reinforced by the Ankara Green City Action Plan (GCAP, 2021), which provides sectoral action pathways and financing strategies. Together, these plans ensure coherence between data reporting, mitigation actions, and long-term sustainable development goals.

The inventory covers the entire jurisdiction boundary of Ankara Metropolitan Municipality, aligning with administrative boundaries and including both urban and peri-urban areas. The population data used for the inventory year is based on official statistics provided by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK). The methodology incorporates activity data from local institutions such as ASKİ (Ankara Water and Sewerage Administration), EGO (Electricity, Gas and Bus Operations Organization), and relevant municipal directorates (e.g., disaster management, health services, strategy departments), as well as affiliated companies and industrial zones. Collaboration with external stakeholders, including universities (notably Middle East Technical University - METU), professional chambers, organized industrial zones, and rural services, was essential in compiling accurate and sector-specific data.

The emissions inventory encompasses a wide range of sectors, including:

Energy supply and use: electricity consumption, heating and cooling, and energy use in public facilities.

Transportation: private vehicles, public transport systems, freight, and non-motorized mobility.

Buildings: residential, commercial, and public buildings, with attention to energy efficiency and heating systems.

Waste management: solid waste disposal, landfill gas, waste treatment, and recycling initiatives.

Water supply and wastewater management: pumping, treatment, and distribution operations.

Cross-cutting sectors: food security, biodiversity, green spaces, and rural activities, including agricultural support such as distribution of drought-resistant seeds and solar irrigation systems.

Emission factors used in the inventory are primarily drawn from the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories, ensuring alignment with international standards. Where available, national and local emission factors were used to reflect the specific energy mix and waste composition of Ankara. Global warming potential (GWP) values were taken from the IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5, 2013). The gases included in the inventory are carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), and nitrous oxide (N₂O), which together account for the majority of urban GHG emissions.

The tool used to compile the inventory was developed internally by Ankara Metropolitan Municipality with support from consultancy and academic partners, relying on spreadsheet-based calculations following GPC and CRF requirements. This internal process allowed for consistency with local data sources and flexibility in integrating sector-specific information. The inventory has undergone internal review for accuracy and coherence across sectors. Although not externally verified, the inventory was cross-checked with data from national and international sources to ensure credibility and reliability.

The inventory not only provides a baseline of current emissions but also supports long-term climate planning by identifying high-emission sectors, enabling targeted actions, and tracking progress over time. It is directly connected with Ankara's strategic commitments under the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM), the Green City Program, and Turkey's national climate strategies. In addition, it contributes to multiple international frameworks, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities, and SDG 13: Climate Action), and aligns with the principles of TCFD (Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures) for transparency in climate data reporting. 
Supporting documents that provide additional methodological details and sectoral actions include:
•	Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP, 2021) - https://s.ankara.bel.tr/files/2025/08/15/f42313fc846b7ea1e79493e25be5e4d7.pdf
•	Ankara Green City Action Plan (GCAP, 2021) - https://www.ankara.bel.tr/files/2022/06/22/e6828f0c69930859c92414b0657fa2cd.pdf

Funding for an extensive program of enhancements supported by an external technical specialist was obtained in 2023 and a contract awarded in November 2024 after an open tender process, the first for this exercise. Previous iterations have either been internal or grant funded.

The service provider has developed new accounting tools to address the many data challenges that occur at local level jurisdictions in developing countries. Methodologies have been revised to better integrate newer higher quality data sources such as the survey of larger scheduled emitters (SAGERS) by the Department of Forestry Fisheries and the Environment with older sources and insights from stakeholder engagement with the oil industry. Significantly, the service provider has increased the scope of the inventory to BASIC+ through estimating AFOLU and IPPU emissions, including the significant contribution of demand-side HFCs from air-conditioning units. In certain cases, assumptions, such as transmission loss factors have been reviewed, introducing significant changes. Additionally, the reporting year, 2023 saw very large step changes in the energy system, foremost amongst them extreme levels of power cuts imposed by the national system operator with some level of national load curtailment being imposed for 6335 hours and customers being disconnected on average for 792 hours during the year. As a result of this national supply crisis, the large peaking plant within the jurisdiction operated at a very high capacity factor. This combined with the accelerating recovery of the aviation industry after COVID and the resumption of full operations by the local refinery after a fire related closure, caused petroleum fuel energy use to increase within the jurisdiction even while electricity demand was severely impaired. 

While there are continuous improvements in the quality of data and estimation methodologies for internal operations, and for the sectors which the City has its own data such as solid waste, wastewater, and electricity (CCT electricity sales data), there continues to be inconsistencies in the data collected from external stakeholders (national entities in particular). Our dependence on these data sources for key sectors such as transport, and a proportion of electricity consumption supplied by the national distribution subsidiary of state utility, Eskom, remain ongoing challenges.

The City of Cape Town (CCT) CIRIS GHG inventory is reporting a 2023 base year for 2025 CDP reporting. The 2023 base year results are based on updates of key sector datasets that are readily accessible, such as CCT Electricity sales data, national liquid fuels by trade category, solid waste, wastewater and population. The rest of the data is scaled with the appropriate methodologies based on the aforementioned newly developed accounting tools. The City publishes a Cape Town State of Energy and Carbon Report every 5 years as a detailed analysis, which requires significant resources. The City is currently conducting the next update of the CT State of Energy and Carbon report which will include a detailed revision of all data domains, with base year 2023/2024, and documentation of new accounting methodologies. 

The City is committed to transparent and full scientific methodologies as such we have an extensive list of data products and archives. Additionally we have a detailed workbook that illustrates how each calculation was made and with all assumption used. This Outputs database as well the State of Energy and Carbon Report is available here: https://odp-cctegis.opendata.arcgis.com/content/46c2d508166042d0acac9ae87d528e9b/about .The City's historical inventories have been attached, and are available on the City's Open Data Portal: https://odp-cctegis.opendata.arcgis.com/content/083e44674f7c4e8cb23131d1c02c8afa/about

The GHG emissions categories and inventory methodology for the City of San Diego are based on the U.S. Communities Protocol, which requires five basic emissions-generating activities to be included in a Community GHG inventory. These categories are generally recognized as being under the collective control and management of the community whereas other emissions-generating activities such as air travel or shipping are not considered as such. Therefore, allocating emissions from these categories is better handled at a higher geographic level of aggregation. Aviation, rail, and waterborne navigation activities and emissions are not within the jurisdiction of the City of San Diego but are the responsibility of other public agencies, and therefore included in GHG inventories for those entities (including the San Diego Regional Association of Governments, San Diego Unified Port District, and others).

column30:
The city-wide GHG emissions inventory for 2024 was developed in accordance with the Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventories (GPC) and its associated guidelines. The inventory incorporates new emission sources, including fuel oil, district cooling, and process emissions from wastewater treatment plants.

Transportation emissions were refined to include 50% of transboundary trips for on-road (using Google EIE data) and aviation, consistent with GPC guidance to ensure emissions within jurisdictional boundaries are appropriately represented.

Wastewater treatment plant emissions were estimated using the Local Government Operations Protocol (LGOP) and the U.S. Inventory of Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Sinks. Of the three facilities serving the city, two are located within the jurisdictional boundary.
Indirect emissions from wastewater treatment, airport ground operations, and solid waste-generating activities are included under stationary sources. Because solid waste disposal facilities are located outside city limits, only emissions from in-jurisdiction activities occurring beyond the boundary are accounted for.

These methodological updates did not require recalculation of historical inventories, though the city is evaluating whether to update past inventories to reflect the refinements introduced in 2024.

Overall, the 2024 city-wide inventory maintains consistency with GPC standards, ensuring transparency, accuracy, and comparability in emissions reporting.

This year, changes were made to the methodology used to calculate the municipality's emissions inventory in order to more closely comply with the European guidelines set out in the latest version of the Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Inventories. 

This inventory continues to follow the Common Reporting Format, including CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions in the Stationary Energy, Transport, Waste and Wastewater, IPPU and AFOLU sectors, as well as distributing them across scopes 1, 2 and 3. 

The biggest change compared to previous inventories is the source of data for the electricity emission factor, which is now provided by the Portuguese Environment Agency (APA), the entity that publishes the annual national inventories. This has also become the data source for emission factors associated with other energy vectors, in line with IPCC 2006, considering the 2019 Refinement. 

In addition, there have been changes, namely to the methodology for accounting for electricity losses (scope 3 of Stationary Energy), the calculation of fugitive emissions from natural gas, and the methodology for calculating emissions associated with the disposal of solid waste in landfills, now following a First Order Decay model (FOD) recommended by GPC. 

The attached file corresponds to the 2023 emissions inventory in tCO2 equivalent. The document also identifies the respective emission factors (in tCO2e/GWh) and activity data.

column15: The 2024 greenhouse gas inventory of Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality was prepared in line with the 2006 IPCC Guidelines and the Local GHG Mitigation methodology of the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change. Emissions were assessed under three scopes: direct emissions (Scope 1), indirect emissions from electricity/heat consumption (Scope 2), and other indirect emissions such as supply chain and waste management (Scope 3). The inventory covered stationary energy (residential, commercial, public, industrial, agricultural, and street lighting), transport (road, rail, air, etc.), waste, industrial processes and product use (IPPU), and agriculture-forestry-land use (AFOLU). Data sources included municipal records, national/local statistics, National emission factors, Ministry of Agriculture inventories, and local waste/biogas facilities. Standard IPCC emission factors were applied, with Tier 1 calculations conducted in line with the national greenhouse gas inventory. The IPCC notation system (0, NE, NA, IE) was used. This ensures comparability between the 2015 BEI, 2020 MEI, and 2024 MEI inventories. Notably, land use was excluded in 2015 and 2020 but included in 2024. Unit conversions and supporting documentation were provided as annexes.\n

The unit conversion factors are provided in the attached Excel file, while the emission conversion factors and data sources are additionally included in the YSGEA Excel file. 
Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality's 2024 greenhouse gas emission inventory was prepared based on the internationally recognized 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories methodology and in line with the Local Greenhouse Gas Emission Reduction (LGGER) calculation methodology provided by the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change of the Republic of Türkiye.

In the study, emissions were evaluated under three main categories: direct emissions (Scope 1), indirect emissions from electricity and heat consumption (Scope 2), and other indirect emissions such as those from the supply chain and waste management (Scope 3). In this way, both emissions resulting from local fuel consumption and those associated with citywide energy use and other indirect effects were separately calculated.

The preparation process of the inventory was supported by the relevant units of Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality, including the Department of Environmental Protection, Zero Waste and Climate Change - Zero Waste Branch, the Department of Transportation, GASKİ (Gaziantep Water and Sewerage Administration), the Department of Agricultural Services, the Department of Support Services, and Gazi Ulaş (urban transportation authority).

The scope of the inventory study was kept quite broad, and greenhouse gas emissions from various sectors of the city were examined in detail. Within this framework, the following sectors were included in the report: stationary energy (residential, commercial and public buildings, industrial facilities, agriculture, and street lighting), transportation (road, rail, maritime, air, and off-road vehicles), waste (solid waste management, biological treatment, waste incineration, wastewater treatment), industrial processes and product use, and agriculture-forestry-land use (AFOLU).

column30:
Este ano houve alterações à metodologia de contabilização do inventário de emissões do município, de forma a responder de forma mais aproximada às orientações europeias contempladas na versão mais recente do Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Inventories. 
Este inventário continua a seguir o Common Reporting Format, incluindo emissões de CO2, CH4 e N2O, nos setores da Energia Estacionária, Transportes, Resíduos e Águas Residuais, IPPU e AFOLU, assim como distribui as mesmas pelos âmbitos 1, 2 e 3. 
A maior alteração relativamente aos inventários antigos é a fonte de dados do fator de emissão da eletricidade, sendo atualmente utilizado o fator disponibilizado pela Agência Portuguesa do Ambiente (APA), entidade que publica os inventários nacionais anuais. Esta também passou a ser a fonte de dados dos fatores de emissão associados a outros vetores energéticos, em linha com o IPCC 2006, considerando o Refinement de 2019. 
Para além disto, houve alterações, nomeadamente à metodologia de contabilização das perdas de eletricidade (âmbito 3 da Energia Estacionária), ao cálculo das emissões fugitivas de gás natural, à metodologia de cálculo das emissões associadas à deposição de resíduos sólidos urbanos em aterro, seguindo agora o modelo de decaimento (FOD) recomendado pelo GPC.
O ficheiro anexado corresponde ao inventário de emissões de 2023 em tCO2 equivalente. No documento são também identificados os respetivos fatores de emissão (em tCO2e/GWh) e os dados de atividade.

column30: Although HFCs, PFCs, and SF6 were not included in the total emissions, they were still included in the 2021 GHG emissions inventory report under community non-energy emissions for informational purposes only. “To be consistent with previous 2010, 2019, and 2020 GHG emissions inventories, the 2021 Community-wide GHG Inventory accounts for only one non-energy related GHG emission, leakage of fugitive emissions from the community natural gas consumption. These non-energy emissions come from anthropogenic sources like waste treatment facilities, transportation, industrial processes, and climate control in buildings. However, this inventory, includes, as information only, additional non-energy emissions not directly related to energy production or consumption. Emissions from non-energy sources include halogenated gases, leakage from natural gas transmission and distribution, and waste management. While non-energy emissions include various GHGs, hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) are one of the GHG gases of greatest concern due to their widespread use and significantly higher global warming potential than carbon dioxide. Given their extensive use in air conditioning, refrigeration, and spray cans, HFCs are closely monitored” (2021 FTL Inventory Report p. 6). \n\nIn addition, the City's Press Play Strategic Plan 2029 has a stated objective to “Grow and Enhance the Urban Forest.” The City has stated goals to enhance its tree canopy to 33% by 2040.” Since 2021, the City has sequestered 43,390 MT CO2e from an urban forest coverage of now 26.6%. This has been accounted for as negative emissions in the total Community Greenhouse Gas Emissions by Sector and Source in Calendar Year 2021.

The greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory undertaken by Davao City marks a critical milestone in the city's climate action journey, serving as the first comprehensive effort to measure emissions across key sectors. With no prior inventory to reference, this initiative establishes the baseline data needed to guide evidence-based planning and decision-making. The absence of historical records highlights the importance of adopting a rigorous, transparent, and data-driven approach to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the city's emissions profile.

Recognizing that climate action requires consistent monitoring and evaluation, Davao City is committed to regularly updating its GHG inventory. This iterative process ensures that the city can track progress, identify trends, and recalibrate mitigation strategies in response to evolving challenges. More importantly, the GHG inventory is not a standalone activity but is fully integrated into the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP), which serves as a dynamic roadmap for achieving long-term sustainability and resilience.

By institutionalizing GHG inventory updates, Davao City reaffirms its dedication to proactive climate governance, ensuring that policies and programs remain responsive to scientific data and global best practices. This commitment strengthens the city's vision of becoming a globally livable and climate-resilient city, demonstrating leadership in local climate action while contributing to national and international sustainability goals.

In conjunction with the Malaysian Government's voluntary efforts to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, Iskandar Malaysia — as a leading economic development region — has proactively implemented the Low Carbon Society (LCS) framework since 2005. As part of this commitment, Iskandar Malaysia has completed all six stages of the Low Carbon Development Cycle, including Stage 6: Tracking Performance, which involves regular GHG inventory assessments to monitor mitigation progress and identify emissions contributions across major sectors.

The region developed its first regional-scale GHG inventories using Basic Reporting for the periods 2015-2017 and 2018-2019, covering five sectors: Stationary Energy, Transportation, Waste, Industrial Processes and Product Use (IPPU), and Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use (AFOLU). These inventories currently track emissions from CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O, and plans are underway to expand coverage to include HFCs, PFCs, SF₆, and NF₃ in the next reporting cycle.

In alignment with the Low Carbon Society Blueprint for Iskandar Malaysia 2030 and national priorities under the National Carbon Market Policy, the GHG inventory is scheduled for updating every four years. As part of this, the Johor State Government, under the Johor Green Deal policy, is currently preparing a dedicated budget to support the development of a comprehensive Greenhouse Gas Inventory for the year 2024/2025. This inventory will cover Iskandar Malaysia and the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), and aims to provide high-resolution data to inform policy, climate finance, and ESG-aligned infrastructure planning.

column30:
Comment on methodology:
Scope 2, stationary energy, is calculated with local energy data from Statistics Sweden and local emission factors for district heating and national emission factor for electricity. 

Within Helsingborg's heating sector, district heating is the most common form of heating. Climate emissions resulting from district heating use are calculated similarly for electricity based on an emission factor corresponding to the fuel mix found in the district heating network. Today, these emissions mainly come from the system's cogeneration production, which releases both biogenic and fossil carbon dioxide because of energy recovery from waste destruction.

The emission factor used for electricity 2023 is calculated by “Boverket” The Swedish National Board of Housing, Building and Planning for the period 2015-2017. It considered production in Sweden, taking into account imports and exports. Average for the period was 37 g CO2e/kWh. 

Emission data for scope 1 stationary energy, transport, waste, AFOLU and IPPU are retrieved from the Swedish national emission database which is established through a collaboration through IVL Swedish Environmental Institute, SCB Statistics Sweden, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU) and the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological institute (SMHI). Emission data and emission factors from the national emission database includes CO2, CH4, N2O, SF6, HFC and PFC. The database offers emissions at a local level. The geographical distribution is mainly carried out according to the “top-down” concept. Emissions for Sweden have been distributed across the country in a grid where the squares correspond to 1 km². The distribution is done using relevant statistics and geographical data, such as road networks, pastures, harvested forests and population data. The Methodologies used for the database are in accordance with the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories. 

For 2023 emissions from leakage from landfills are measured by the municipality owned waste company NSR. Emissions from work machines in the port of Helsingborg (included in off road transport) are calculated by the Port of Helsingborg.

column30:
Brighton & Hove City Council uses the UK government Local authority GHG estimates in its annual reporting, as the data is more up to date than the SCATTER data used here. We have uploaded our 2023 GHG Emissions Inventory under 'Additional inventories', with the latest data from DESNZ. However the LA GHG data set is not compatible with GCOM requirements. So on this occasion, SCATTER data has been used instead. 

Our total GHG emissions as reported for the year 2023, are lower than our last reported year of 2020. The reduction in reported emissions is due, in part, to the reductions of GHG emissions from Domestic energy, Transport and Waste Sectors, and in part to differences in methodology (for example, the omission of scope 3 emissions estimates in 2023 DESNZ data set).
We previously reported scope 3 emissions provided by SCATTER but, following the termination of their funding, no update has been provided beyond 2020. This omission has deflated our estimate of the city's total emissions, in particular due to the omission of Scope 3 emissions from Stationary Energy and Aviation as previously reported by SCATTER.

Em 2016, submeteu o Plano de Ação para a Sustentabilidade Energética e Climática (PASEC) com os objetivos para 2030 (agora revisado em 2024 com metas atualizadas, e aprovado em assembleia municipal) , e a também revisada Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (EMAAC). Após a submissão destes documentos, o Município comprometeu-se a apresentar, bianualmente, relatórios de acompanhamento da implementação das medidas apresentadas. Neste sentido, Guimarães já submeteu relatórios de acompanhamento que permitem avaliar a evolução tendo em vista os objetivos estabelecidos, em termos de redução das emissões de CO2, consumos de energia e implementação de ações de adaptação. Atualmente, novos projetos fazem parte da agenda climática de Guimarães. Guimarães foi selecionada para a Missão das 100 cidades inteligentes e neutras em termos de clima até 2030, a chamada “Missão Cidades” da União Europeia\'. No âmbito do programa europeu de investigação e inovação Horizonte Europa, tem como objetivo tornar 100 cidades europeias inteligentes e climaticamente neutras até 2030.Com a implementação desta visão desde 2013, o município foi já capaz de introduzir diversas medidas de promoção da sustentabilidade, mitigação e adaptação às alterações climáticas. De uma forma global, estas já permitiram reduzir o consumo de energia e das emissões de CO2. \nAo dia de hoje Guimarães já se encontra com o seu \'Climate City Contract (CCC)\' aprovado pela união europeia. \nPor estar integrado nas demais iniciativas de reporte, e estando estas desfasadas em diferentes momentos, por vezes, podem haver ligeiras alterações nos valores dos inventários de emissões. column30: 2000年代初，台灣政府傾向於建立溫室氣體盤查方法。但是，由於各市排放類別、計算方法、活動數據的選擇、數據來源等方面的差異，導致其缺乏客觀性。 為此，環境保護署（EPA）提出了《城市級溫室氣體清單指南》，清單遵循政府間氣候變化專門委員會（IPCC）制定的國際地方政府溫室氣體排放分析協議（IEAP）。 《城市級溫室氣體清單指南》不僅遵循了溫室氣體清單的五個基本原則：相關性、完整性、一致性、準確性和透明度，而且與國際趨勢高度接軌。在這種情況下，該方法被認為是每個城市減少溫室氣體的自我評估，並且在國際上是可檢查和可驗證的。就清單氣體而言，HFCs、PFCs 和 NF3 也被列入清單。 然而，台灣政府禁止使用 HFC 和 PFC，因此排放量為零。 NF3為半導體產業排放，屏東縣無相關企業，因此排放量為零。 因此，沒有 HFC、PFC 和 NF3 排放。In the early 2000s, Taiwan's government tended to build a method for GHG inventory. However, the lack of objectivity results from the differences in the emission categories, calculation methods, selection of activity data, and data sources of the municipalities. Therefore, the＂Guidelines for City Level Greenhouse Gas Inventories＂ were proposed by the Environmental Protection Administration (EPA), and the inventory followed the International Local Government Greenhouse Gas Emissions Analysis Protocol (IEAP) by Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). The＂Guidelines for City Level Greenhouse Gas Inventories＂not only followed the five basic principles of greenhouse gas inventories: relevance, completeness, consistency, accuracy, and transparency are also highly connected to the international trend. In this case, the method is considered a self-assessment of reducing GHG for each city and being inspectable and verifiable internationally. As far as inventoried gas is concerned, HFCs, PFCs, and NF3 are also included in the list. Nevertheless, HFCs and PFCs are prohibited by Taiwan Government. NF3 is emitted by semiconductor industry, and there is no related company in Pingtung County. As a consequence, the HFCs, PFCs, and NF3 emission is zero.

column30:
Historically, emissions have been reported by the SCATTER Tool, which was discontinued officially this year. York's SCATTER reports for 2019 and 2020 are attached as historical inventories here, and as guided by CDP are in line with the requirements to align with the CRF and report on Scope 1, 2 and 3. Following the discontinuation of SCATTER, City of York Council have adopted the accredited official statistics from the UK's Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, 'UK local authority and regional greenhouse gas emissions statistics, 2005 to 2023'. This data has been categorized by Scope 1, 2 and 3 data. 
Scope 1:
Direct emissions from sources within the city's boundary (e.g., city-owned vehicles, combustion in buildings). 
Scope 2:
Indirect emissions from the consumption of purchased electricity, heating, and cooling within the city's boundary. 
Scope 3 (City-Wide):
All other indirect emissions that happen outside the city's physical boundary but are a result of activities within the city, as well as transboundary emissions related to the use of goods and services consumed by its residents and businesses. The data set provides a spatial disaggregation of territorial carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from the UK GHG Inventory
(GHGI), part of the National Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (NAEI).

 SCATTER was underpinned by point source data from the Department for Energy, Security and Net Zero. National end user emissions data are used to calculate emission factors for each activity. Local authority activity data are then multiplied by the relevant emission factor to generate an estimate of emissions in each LA. More information on SCATTER is available here https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/667ad7a7c7f64e234208ffc2/local-authority-ghg-technical-report-2022.pdf 

Both of these inventory processes have been internally approved, as seen in the publically available papers below. The lastest published inventory has also been internally audited by CYC's owned auditor organisation. The DESNZ statistics are officially accredited. 
Background paper: York Emissions Inventory Report 2024
https://democracy.york.gov.uk/documents/s179439/EMDS_City%20Wide%20Emissions%202024.pdf 

Background paper: York Emissions Inventory Report 2023 
https://modgov.york.gov.uk/documents/s171184/York%20Emissions%20Inventory%20Report%202023.pdf 

Background paper: York Emissions Inventory Report 2022
https://modgov.york.gov.uk/documents/s164308/EMDS%20City%20Emissions%20Dec%202022.pdf 

Background paper: York Emissions Inventory Report 2021 
https://modgov.york.gov.uk/documents/s153498/EMDS_York%20Emisions%20Inventory%20Report_2021.pdf 

As such, in line with the CDP 2025 requirements, the most recent invetory provides a information from 2021 or later, and the historical reports from SCATTER can also be observed as required.

Based on the given data, Baguio City's GHG emissions (by ADB and Baguio city's Comprehensive Development Plan) mainly come from:
1. Energy (53%) - This includes emissions from electricity generation, heating, cooking, lighting, etc. A majority of Baguio's energy comes from fossil fuels like coal and oil, resulting in carbon dioxide and methane emissions;
2. Transportation (20%) - Gasoline and diesel vehicles emit carbon dioxide and air pollutants. Asan urban center, Baguio has a high usage of motorized transport
3. Waste disposal (13%) - Decaying organic waste in landfills produces methane, a potent GHG. Improper solid waste management causes these emissions;
4. Wastewater treatment (13%) - Microbial breakdown of sewage produces methane and nitrous oxide emissions; and
5. Land cover change (1%) - Baguio has experienced rapid urbanization. Changing natural lands to agricultural or urban use releases stored carbon.
*The attached PDF of the main community-wide emissions inventory is the only version currently available and has been reviewed and submitted to the city council.

El inventario reportado en 2025, corresponde a un Inventario de Gases de Efecto Invernadero desarrollado por el programa HuellaChile del Ministerio del Medio Ambiente (organismo gubernamental), que estima las emisiones desagregadas por comuna, de todas las comunas de la región metropolitana del año 2022 (año base). En este inventario se detallan las emisiones específicas de Peñalolén por cada subsector y alcance, del nivel Básico de la metodología GPC.

Three inventories—2015, 2018, and 2024—have been completed to date. Apart from 2015 inventory, all follow the GPC BASIC+ reporting level, covering Scopes 1, 2, and 3.
2015 and 2018 Inventories: These covered the entire administrative jurisdiction of Dire Dawa, including both urban and rural areas. Consequently, sectors with significant rural influence—particularly stationary energy (biomass and kerosene for cooking) and agriculture, forestry, and other land use (AFOLU)—showed higher emissions.
2024 Inventory: This latest assessment focuses solely on the urban boundary of Dire Dawa City. This change brings the inventory scope in line with the C40 methodology for city-scale GHG accounting, and aligns with the functional urban area targeted in this Climate Action Plan. As a result, apparent reductions in some sectors reflect a revised spatial boundary rather than actual mitigation outcomes.

column30: The 2020 GHG emissions inventory was prepared using the best available data for each emissions category and does not include on-road transportation. The activity data for electricity, natural gas, solid waste, and water sectors are based on tracked and observed usage for the year and therefore, correctly reflect the impacts of Covid-19. However, for on-road transportation, the vehicle miles traveled (VMT) data are estimates from the SANDAG activity based model (ABM). The most recent SANDAG activity based model, ABM2+, was last calibrated with observed data from 2016 and forecasts 2020 VMT. While transportation historically accounts for the largest share of GHG emissions in an inventory, the forecasted VMT does not take into account the impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic and cannot be updated to provide 2020 VMT data for each jurisdiction. Caltrans PeMS data provides observed regional VMT on freeways for 2020. Image 1 compares the observed VMT on freeways in the San Diego region for the years 2019, 2020 and 2021. The observed data is only available for freeway and it cannot be scaled down to individual jurisdictions which have different confguration of roads. While other sources of data and anecdotal experience show lower VMT in 2020, there is no data for how each jurisdiction's VMT changed during 2020. The Caltrans PeMS data set shows similar travel trends in 2021 as in 2019 which suggests that lower VMT in 2020 is likely due to the impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic and may not sustain long term.

Este ano houve alterações à metodologia de contabilização do inventário de emissões do município, de forma a responder de forma mais aproximada às orientações europeias contempladas na versão mais recente do Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Inventories. 
Este inventário continua a seguir o Common Reporting Format, incluindo emissões de CO2, CH4 e N2O, nos setores da Energia Estacionária, Transportes, Resíduos e Águas Residuais, IPPU e AFOLU, assim como distribui as mesmas pelos âmbitos 1, 2 e 3. 
A maior alteração relativamente aos inventários antigos é a fonte de dados do fator de emissão da eletricidade, sendo atualmente utilizado o fator disponibilizado pela Agência Portuguesa do Ambiente (APA), entidade que publica os inventários nacionais anuais. Esta também passou a ser a fonte de dados dos fatores de emissão associados a outros vetores energéticos, em linha com o IPCC 2006, considerando o Refinement de 2019. 
Para além disto, houve alterações, nomeadamente à metodologia de contabilização das perdas de eletricidade (âmbito 3 da Energia Estacionária), ao cálculo das emissões fugitivas de gás natural, à metodologia de cálculo das emissões associadas à deposição de resíduos sólidos urbanos em aterro, seguindo agora o modelo de decaimento (FOD) recomendado pelo GPC.
O ficheiro anexado corresponde ao inventário de emissões de 2023 em tCO2 equivalente. No documento são também identificados os respetivos fatores de emissão (em tCO2e/GWh) e os dados de atividade.

column30: Inventories are calculated two years in arrears due to availability of national data; therefore this inventory is for 2022 and published in 2025. Cornwall Council commission the University of Exeter to carry out the inventory on an annual basis. The inventory provides a time series of greenhouse gas emissions by sector and charting progress and informing the development of a trajectory to net zero carbon. The inventories have been updated to incorporate enhancements to methodology to improve completeness of reporting where possible. For Cornwall in 2022, total emissions slightly increased to 3,458 kt CO2e, a <1% increase from 2021, but a 29% decrease from 4,851 kt CO2e in 2008. The largest percentage change was for marine navigation, where emissions increased by 72% (19 kt CO2e) from 2021 to 2022, mainly due to the new methodology to estimate emissions from fishing vessels from 2022 onwards. Methodology changes also affected aviation emissions, which increased by 36% (11 kt CO2e) due to methodology changes in the underlying data and continued removal of COVID-19 travel restrictions. Road transport emissions have also continued to rise as a result of removing COVID-19 travel restrictions, increasing by 8% (74 kt CO2e) and returning to pre-pandemic levels. Emissions from stationary energy in residential and commercial/industrial buildings recorded an 8% (56 ktCO2e) and 2% (12 ktCO2e) reduction respectively, due to the decarbonisation of grid electricity and lower fuel demand in response to warmer temperatures and rising energy prices. Agricultural emissions also decreased by 2% (18 kt CO2e), largely due to a decrease in nitrous oxide emissions from agricultural soils resulting from reduced fertiliser use.\nModest reductions in emissions were observed in other sectors with the most material absolute reduction coming from industrial processes and product use (12% or 8 ktCO2e). Reductions in rail transport (3%) and waste (<1%) were all below 7 ktCO2e.

column30: The community-wide GHG emissions inventory has been populated using the CityInSight model, which is a tool and service developed by Sustainability Solutions Group (SSG) who are the consultants on the Town of Whitby's Climate Emergency Response Plan. CityInSight is a community energy and emissions model with integrated spatially-explicit land-use and transportation components, and stocks-and-flows accounting. The model enables bottom-up accounting for energy supply and demand, including energy sources (e.g., renewables, coal, oil, gas), energy consuming stocks (e.g., vehicles, appliances, dwellings) and all intermediate energy flows. It captures the actual consumption data and associated emissions associated with electricity, natural gas, transportation, waste management, etc. on a community-level.Additionally, CityInSight incorporates the Global GHG Protocol for Cities, a GHG accounting framework launched as the new global standard by the World Resources Institute, ICLEI, C40, UN Habitat and others at the UN Conference of the Parties in Lima in 2014. CityInSight has a web interface and many applications, helping cities to determine the best plans and actions to take on the path to sustainable, low carbon communities.As a part of the next update of Whitby's Climate Emergency Response Plan Phase 2: Mitigation, a BASIC+ inventory covering HFCs, PFCs, SF6, and NF3 gases will be conducted. Additionally the emissions inventory will be updated using emissions factors from the IPCC Sixth, Fifth, or Fourth Assessment Reports.

column30: The Denizli Greenhouse Gas Inventory has been prepared in accordance with the Global Protocol for Community-Scale GHG Inventories (GPC). Moreover, the final inventory report was prepared based on the common reporting framework (CRF) of the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM).In this way, the results described in the inventory report are intended to be comparable and acceptable on a global scale. The inventory prepared at the urban scale includes all the emission sources within the borders of the Denizli Metropolitan Municipality. Denizli Metropolitan Municipality's authority covers the Denizli province's provincial boundaries. The inventory content is based on the classification of emission sources set by GPC. When preparing inventory in the framework of GPC, the scope of the inventory was determined depending on the detail, accuracy, and reliability of the available data. During the preparation of the inventory, all emission sources within the borders of the authority of the municipality were scanned, and the maximum amount of data was tried to be collected. The inventory only covered Scope 1 - Direct Emissions and Scope 2 - Indirect Emissions of the GPC. However, the emissions under Scope 3 - Indirect (Consumption Based) Emissions were not included in the inventory due to the fact that it is very difficult to reach related data. According to the results of the GPC approach, the total greenhouse gas emissions of Denizli province for the year 2016 were estimated to be 7.5 million tons of CO2e. This amount refers to 7.5 tons of CO2e per capita, which was proportional to the population of Denizli in the same year (1.005.687), and this number was higher than Turkey's 2016 average calculated as 6.3 tons of CO2e per capita. The total emissions of Denizli within Türkiye's total emissions in 2016 constituted 1.5%. Denizli MM updated the province-wide GHG Inventory in October 2022. This CDP reporting consists of the results of this updated inventory for 2020. (Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Denizli MM was unable to prepare its 2018 inventory which was supposed to be prepared in 2020.) According to this updated inventory, the total emission of Denizli MM for 2020 was 6.9 million tons of CO2e, and per-capita emission was 6.6 tons of CO2e. According to these results, the total emissions of Denizli MM decreased considerably in 4 years. The biggest decreases were the results of reduced coal consumption which was replaced with natural gas, and a major drop in industrial processes sourced emissions.

column30:
Se estimaron las emisiones del municipio de La Democracia, Escuintla, para el año base 2,022. Para realizar los cálculos se utilizó información generada y/o proporcionada por diferentes instituciones tales como el Ministerio de Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (MARN), Ministerio de Agricultura y Ganadería (MAGA), Ministerio de Energía y Minas (MEM), Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE), la Superintendencia de Administración Tributaria (SAT), Municipalidad de La Democracia y la Mancomunidad Sureña para el Desarrollo Integral (MASUR), entre otras fuentes consultadas.
La identificación de los principales sectores y actividades de emisión de gases de efecto invernadero, permitirán a La Democracia tomar decisiones estratégicas para un desarrollo sostenible de bajas emisiones. Además, brindará insumos para cumplir con los compromisos nacionales de mitigación y mejorar su resiliencia ante la vulnerabilidad del cambio climático.
Para la estimación de las emisiones se siguieron las recomendaciones del Panel Intergubernamental de Expertos sobre el Cambio Climático (IPCC). En ese sentido, se tomaron en cuenta los sectores de Energía estacionaria, Agricultura, Silvicultura y otros Usos del Suelo (AFOLU), Transporte y Desechos. El sector de Procesos Industriales y Uso de Productos no se tomó en cuenta en la estimación, debido a que su incidencia en el municipio es baja.
Además, se utilizó la Guía para elaboración o actualización de inventarios de emisiones de GEI en ciudades colombianas generada por WWF Colombia1. En la mayoría de los casos, las estimaciones emisión tienen un alcance del tipo 1, tomando en cuenta las emisiones generadas dentro del municipio. Sin embargo, el consumo de energía de la red nacional es del tipo 2, refiriéndose a emisiones generadas fuera de los límites geográficos del municipio, pero que tienen una relación directa a las actividades dentro de dichos límites.

column30:
SUSTAINABLE ENERGY ACTION PLAN, 2011.
The Municipality of Ilion signed the Covenant of Mayors on February 11, 2010, committing to reduce carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions by 20% by 2020. In 2011, the Sustainable Energy Action Plan (SEAP) was drafted with the participation of residents and local stakeholders, as well as in cooperation with the main energy providers. The plan was open for consultation from March 15, 2012, to March 30, 2012, and was subsequently approved by the Municipal Council.
Within the Municipality of Ilion, carbon dioxide emissions were estimated at 364,773 tons of CO2 annually, with a base year of 2008. Approximately 3% of these emissions come from municipal buildings, vehicles, and street lighting, 53% from the residential sector, 9% from the tertiary sector, and 35% from private vehicles. The goal was to reduce total emissions by 20% (73,622 tons of CO2 annually) by the year 2020.
The methodology followed was the calculation of energy consumption per sector, which was included in the Sustainable Energy Action Plan, and the summation of CO2 emissions to calculate the Municipality of Ilion's total Baseline Emission Inventory. The calculation used standard national average CO2 emission factors as calculated by the IPCC (2006) and Eurelectric (2005), as included in the guidelines of the Covenant of Mayors.

column30: In 2019, Çorlu Municipality's community-wide greenhouse gas emissions were approximately 339,420 tons of CO₂e, but by 2025, they had decreased to a certain extent thanks to energy efficiency measures, improvements in transportation infrastructure and progress in waste management. In particular, policies such as insulation practices and increased use of natural gas in residential buildings, widespread use of efficiency projects in industry, modernization of public transport fleets and increased bicycle lanes have contributed to reducing the carbon footprint. In addition, increased recycling rates and waste management activities have also contributed to lower emissions. As a result of these efforts, Çorlu's annual emissions are projected to decline to around 305,000-320,000 tons CO₂e by 2025. However, this reduction must be made sustainable in the face of factors such as increasing population, rapid urbanization and consumption pressure. While the progress achieved in this period demonstrates Çorlu's commitment and capacity to achieve the SECAP targets, it also clearly shows the need for the development of more effective emission reduction policies.

In the past, Hue City had a GHG inventory using the Bilan Carbone method to estimate the GHG inventory of Hue City's Authority. Within the framework of the project “Action towards Resource-efficient and Low Carbon 
Cities in Asia”, this report in the link shown below is made to provide some general information about Hue City and an inventory of GHG emissions in 2010 for all of Hue municipality's activities. For the latter purpose, the related data have been collected from 81 units under the direct administration of Hue City's People's Committee. The final data analysis based on the Bilan Carbone method shows that among the municipality's activities, the travel by employees and all visitors of the municipality is the largest source of GHG emissions (1,824 tonnes equ CO2). Two other 
sectors of the municipality that contribute most to its total GHG emissions are materials 
input and freight, respectively. The analysis of materials inputs, which include incoming 
materials, products, and services purchased, reveals that the GHG emission contribution of 
this sector is 1,813 tonnes equ. CO2, and the largest share of GHG emissions in this sector 
comes from the purchase of building materials. The freight, which comprises “internal 
transports by municipal vehicles”, “incoming vehicles with goods to municipality”, and 
“outgoing vehicles with goods from municipality” is estimated to release 1,462 tonnes. 
CO2e and the largest share of GHG emission in this sector comes from the outgoing freight 
(627 tonnes equ. CO2). Finally, the report attempts to give some explanations for these final analysis outcomes, put forward some plans, and propose some next steps for the city, based on the final analysis outcomes, to raise the population's awareness and to get multi-stakeholders involved in the mitigation of GHG emissions.

Ca Mau Province is currently in the process of implementing Decision No. 13/2024/QĐ-TTg of the Prime Minister. This decision promulgates the list of sectors and greenhouse gas (GHG) emitting facilities that are required to conduct GHG inventories.

Accordingly, these facilities are responsible for:

Conducting the GHG inventory for the year 2024.

Submitting their first GHG inventory report to the provincial People's Committee in 2025.

Therefore, at this stage, the province is in the period during which the designated enterprises are collecting data and preparing their reports. A consolidated provincial-level report can only be prepared after these facility-level data and reports have been received and compiled.

According to information from the Ca Mau Provincial E-Portal, the facilities in the province that are subject to mandatory GHG inventory include:

Ca Mau Petrochemical Power Company (Ca Mau Power Plants 1 and 2)

Ca Mau Fertilizer Joint Stock Company (PVCFC)

Ca Mau Branch of PetroVietnam Gas Corporation

Cong Ly Trading - Service - Tourism Co., Ltd. (Ca Mau City Waste Treatment Plant)

These are major emitters, mainly in the energy, industrial, and waste treatment sectors.

Related action plans

In parallel with initiating the inventory, Ca Mau Province has proactively developed action plans to reduce GHG emissions, showing that the province is preparing on the basis of initial estimates:

Waste management sector: The province has issued an action plan to mitigate GHG emissions in the solid waste management sector.

Target: Reduce GHG emissions in this sector by 18.3% by 2030 compared to the business-as-usual (BAU) scenario (and up to 63.5% with international support).

Actions: The plan includes a specific task to “conduct the inventory and establish the GHG emission boundary for the province's waste sector,” confirming that this is an ongoing and upcoming activity.

In short, the current status of GHG inventory in Ca Mau is that it is in the implementation phase. The province has identified the major emitting facilities that must report, and these facilities are currently preparing their first GHG inventory reports (submission deadline: March 2025).

column30: O Inventário de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (GEE) de Abaetetuba/PA representa o primeiro levantamento sistemático das emissões municipais, identificando as principais fontes de gases como dióxido de carbono (CO₂), metano (CH₄), óxido nitroso (N₂O) e gases industriais fluorados. O inventário atual considera setores como transporte, energia, resíduos sólidos e processos industriais, permitindo quantificar as emissões, subsidiar políticas públicas de mitigação e alinhar o município às metas de redução de emissões da Agenda 2030 e do Pacto Global de Prefeitos pelo Clima e Energia.\nPara o próximo inventário, será incluída a avaliação detalhada do setor AFOLU (Agricultura, Florestas e Outros Usos da Terra), abrangendo atividades como agricultura familiar, manejo florestal, desmatamento, reflorestamento e uso do solo. Essa inclusão permitirá uma análise mais completa das emissões e absorções de carbono no município, reforçando a capacidade de Abaetetuba de planejar ações climáticas integradas e sustentáveis, com foco tanto na mitigação quanto na adaptação às mudanças climáticas.
